newsitem.title: USA: A.G. Edwards lauds Puerto Rico electric bonds.
newsitem.headline: A.G. Edwards lauds Puerto Rico electric bonds.

text.p: Revenue bonds of the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority offer solid invetment-grade credit quality and are an appropriate investment for aggressive fixed-income investors, E.G. Edwards & Sons Inc said in a report.

The report by fixed income research analyst Brian Tournier said the utility is "uniquely positioned" to face deregulation and increased competition because of its physical separation from other power providers, and because the Commonwealth must approve construction of any generating capacity that could compete with the authority, known as PREPA.
"PREPA's customers have no alternative to purchasing power from PREPA, assuring the utility's position as market provider independent of power rate levels," the report said.

The utility produces and supplies virtually all electric power consumed in Puerto Rico, and has 1.25 million customers. Ninety percent of its customers are residential, while sales to those customers account for slightly less than 30 percent of revenues.
Its bonds are secured a 1.2X rate covenant but the utility has generated debt service coverage levels closer to 1.75X in recent years, the report said.

PREPA does face operational and financial challenges from a capital improvement program that calls for spending $1.6 billion through 2000, the report said. The projects are needed to diversify generating resources and help meet demand, and will increase the utility's generating capacity by 38 percent.

The utility has improved operating performance of its generating units in recent years but will need continued strong management to maintain credit quality because of the capital program, the report said.
Standard & Poor's Corp cut its rating on PREPA bonds to BBB-plus from A-minus in August, 1996, citing the "financial and rate implications" of the capital program.
Despite the downgrade, PREPA has demonstrated improving operating and financial results in reent years.

While average customer growth was a modest 1.6 percent annually from 1990 to 1995, energy sales increased by an average of 4.2 percent annually during the period, with commercial power sales increasing even more rapidly at 5.8 percent per year on average.

From 1993 to 1996, PREPA's annual revenues increased at a 5.6 percent average annual rate. Projections through 2000 show growth slowing with annual customer growth and power sales growth expected to average 1.4 percent and 2.5 percent.

Another challenge the utility faces is uncollected receivables from public sector customers, especially Puerto Rico's Aqueduct and Sewer Authority and the Ports Authority, the report said. PREPA's accounts receivable total $300 million or 22 percent of annual revenues, which usually puts it in a low-cash position.
The problem is mitigated by PREPA's ability to tap lines of credit with the Government Development Bank of Puerto Rico.
PRPA's board has exclusive authority to set rates. Its last base rate hike was in 1989 and none are currently planned.
However, average rates are expected to increase almost 25 percent, to about 11.5 cents per kilowatt hour by 2000, because of the substantial costs associated with the capital plan, the report said.

PREPA's rates are already moderatley higher than the national average of about 7 cents per kilowatt hour. Over the next decade, it may face pressure to bring some rate segments in line, especially from manufacturers who will lose tax breaks as Section 936 is phased out.
In addition to the base rate, which reflects operating costs, the rates also include a fuel adjustment component.
PREPA depends on oil for nearly all its generation, and passes on those costs to customers, which can create "significant volatility" in rates in times of changing oil prices, the report said.
By 2000 the new generating capacity will diversify the authority's fuel mix to approximately 19 percent natural gas, 16 percent coal and 2 percent hydro, and 63 percent oil-fired.

Puerto Rico's isolation from other power providers also presents a drawback because the utility cannot purchase power from other utilitites during peak demand times or when generating units are temporarily unavailable.
Therefore it must maintain higher levels of reserve-generating capacity than other utilities.

One of its strategies is to buy power from cogeneration facilities built by corporations on the island. That enables it to avoid taking on new debt to capitalize power plants of its own, and allows it to add both gas and coal generation to its system while reducing dependence on oil.

PREPA bonds are tax-exempt in all 50 states but generally do not offer value on a yield basis because they trade strongly in the market, offering yields closer to A-minus-rated yeild levels, the A.G. Edwards report said.
--Jane Sutton, 305-374-5013
